wachiman.text:
canManage() is granted by the VIEW scope

`canManage()` calls `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`, so an admin who was only given VIEW on all groups passes `requireManage()`. `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` (GroupsResource.java:181) checks only `auth.groups().requireManage()`, which means a view-only group admin can create top-level groups and move groups to the top level. The per-group `canManage(group)` at line 79 correctly accepts only MANAGE. The fix is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)`. Also update the javadoc at GroupPermissionEvaluator.java:75-76, which describes the same wrong rule, and add a negative test (VIEW on all groups, then creating a group returns 403).

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authz resource IDs, not group IDs

Per-group resources are created with `name = groupId` and no type (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:118-121). Only the all-groups resource gets `type = "Groups"` (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:271-274). So `findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` only ever visits the all-groups resource, and two things go wrong:
- `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` looks the resource up by name using its UUID (line 141), finds nothing, and falls back to the type resource.
- `granted.add(groupResource.getId())` adds the authz resource's UUID, not a group ID.

With an all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permission, `UsersResource.searchForUser` then sets `UserModel.GROUPS` to an ID that matches no group, and the JPA subquery (JpaUserProvider.java:762-765) filters out every user. The admin silently sees an empty user list. `getUsersCount` (UsersResource.java:398/425/430) gets the same wrong set. With per-group permissions only, the set is empty: no SQL filter is applied, and `first`/`max` are applied before the `canView` post-filter, so pages come back short. The V1 equivalent (GroupPermissions.java:313-316) maps the resource name back to the group ID. V2 should do the same with `resource.getName()`, and it needs a way to list the per-group resources (for example, set their type, or query policies on the Groups type). The new tests cover only per-group VIEW_MEMBERS, so they don't catch this.

Group removal listener calls a method that V2 makes throw

`management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on (line 67-68). Its `groups()` now returns `GroupPermissionsV2`, whose `setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` (GroupPermissionsV2.java:173-175). The listener is registered when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is on. Can both features be enabled at the same time? If they can, every group deletion would fail inside this listener.

Javadoc for requireManageMembers names the wrong method

The javadoc says it throws if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false, but `requireManageMembers` is the counterpart of `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`. Also, the `@return` at line 145 says "Stream", but the method returns a `Set`.

ES384/ES512 tests use the JDK's default EC curve, so the P-521 / long-form DER path is never exercised

The key pair comes from `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` with no curve set, so all three tests sign with the same default curve. Only the digest changes. `testES512` never uses a P-521 key. That leaves two paths untested. First, the P-521 DER SEQUENCE is longer than 127 bytes, so it takes the long-form length branch in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` (lines 67-79) and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` (lines 137-163). Second, the 66/67-byte r/s handling in `integerToBytes`. Also, the test only round-trips the provider's own decoder and encoder against each other (lines 53-56). A fault shared by both directions would still pass, and nothing checks that the output of `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` is accepted by `Signature.verify`. Suggested fix: generate one key pair per algorithm with `initialize(new ECGenParameterSpec("secp256r1"/"secp384r1"/"secp521r1"))`, then verify `asn1Des` with a JCA `Signature` initialised with the public key.

Two providers with the same order are now picked silently instead of failing

Before this change, finding more than one `CryptoProvider` threw `IllegalStateException`. Now the providers are sorted by `order()` and the first is used. The others are logged only at debug level (lines 64-70). `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200. If a classpath has both the FIPS and the default provider, callers of `CryptoIntegration.init` (`KeycloakApplication`, admin-cli `Globals`, testsuite `CryptoInitRule`) now quietly pick whichever one `ServiceLoader` lists first. That is classpath order, and it can be the non-FIPS one, where before they got a clear error. The Quarkus server is not affected because it calls `setProvider` explicitly (quarkus/runtime/.../KeycloakRecorder.java:214). Suggested fix: keep the old error when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, so the new priority only settles real ties like AuthzClient (100) vs. a full provider (200).

New abstract `order()` breaks any out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation

`order()` is added as an abstract interface method. Every implementation in this repository is updated. Any third-party or custom `CryptoProvider` will fail to compile, or throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` while sorting. A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or another documented baseline) would keep existing implementations working and still let the built-in providers rank themselves.

Dead encoder calls before the real encoding

Lines 114-115 build two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write r and s into them, and throw them away. The returned value comes from the fresh encoders on lines 117-121. These two lines can be removed.

Reader thread is never joined, so the last failures can be missed

The test sets `deletedAll` (line 155) and then checks `caughtExceptions` (line 157) right away, without waiting for the reader thread from line 139. If a `groups(...)` request is still running when the last delete finishes, its exception gets added after the assertion has already passed. That is exactly the race the test is meant to catch. Nothing makes sure the reader runs either: if the thread is scheduled late, the 100 deletes can all finish before it sends a single request, and the test passes without testing anything. The `catch (Exception e)` at line 144 also misses `Error`s such as `AssertionError`. Those end the thread quietly and never get recorded.

To fix it: keep a reference to the `Thread` and call `join()` (with a timeout) before the assertion. Count the reads, or use a latch to wait for the first read before starting the deletes. Catch `Throwable`, or use an `ExecutorService` and check `Future.get()`.

Same NPE is still possible in the paged getSubGroupsStream overloads

The fix guards only `getSubGroupsCount()`. The three paged overloads right above it (lines 256, 262, 268) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check. `modelSupplier` wraps `getGroupModel()` (lines 54, 298-300), which returns null once the group has been deleted from the database. So if a group is deleted while a cached adapter is listing its subgroups, the same `NullPointerException` can still happen. Consider applying the same null handling there (for example, return `Stream.empty()`) so the PR covers every place in this class where a concurrent delete can cause the NPE.

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments does not exist, so the services module won't compile

`UsernameForm.authenticate` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only declaration is `UsernamePasswordForm.isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160), and a repository-wide search finds no no-arg overload. That is a compile error in `services`.

Suggested fix: pass the user, e.g. `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`. That fix also needs the predicate problem on UsernamePasswordForm.java:161 sorted out first.

Passkeys conditional UI now only shows when a user is already identified, so normal first-time login loses it

`isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` returns `... && user != null`. Before this change, both call sites filled the WebAuthn form only when the user was *not* yet known:
- the old `authenticate` filled it in the `else` branch (user == null);
- the old `challenge` checked `context.getUser() == null && ...`.

Now `authenticate` (line 115) and `challenge` (line 137) call `fillContextForm` only when `context.getUser() != null`. So on an ordinary login where no user is set yet:
- `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI` and the challenge are never set, and the passkey option is gone from the username/password page.
- After an invalid-user error (`testInvalidUser` → `challenge`, AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator.java:105-111) the passkeys stay hidden as well.

This breaks tests this PR keeps or adds. For example, `passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey` asserts `//form[@id='webauth']` on a fresh login (PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.java:146), and so do the new tests at lines 196 and 238.

The re-authentication fix needs passkeys in *both* cases. Suggested predicate: `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`, plus whatever per-user restriction is intended when `user != null`.

`reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` turns passkeys off for the realm, so it never tests a user without a passkey

The comment at line 304 says passkeys should not be offered "as this user does not have passkey". But the test sets `setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE)`, so passkeys are hidden for every user because of the realm setting.

The case that matters for this change is not covered: passkeys enabled in the realm, and a re-authenticating user who has only a password. It is also the case most affected by the new `user != null` logic, and by `UsernameForm` no longer skipping the form during re-authentication.

Suggestion: add a variant with passkeys enabled for `test-user@localhost`, or reword the comment.

The `try { assertThat(..., nullValue()); fail(); } catch (Exception)` absence check is convoluted

`findElement` throws `NoSuchElementException` when the element is absent, so `assertThat(..., nullValue())` can never pass. The check works only because `fail()` throws an `AssertionError`, which `catch (Exception)` does not catch.

The Organization test in this same PR uses a clearer form: `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, () -> driver.findElement(...))`. It would read better here (lines 291-296 and 312-317), and catching `Exception` broadly could also hide unrelated failures.

Add `@Override` to `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators`

This method overrides `WebAuthnAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` (WebAuthnAuthenticator.java:128). Without `@Override`, a later rename or signature change in the parent would silently stop the override from applying.

Unhealthy flusher processes are no longer killed before a replacement starts

The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. The new code only kills when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. Processes come from `self.mp_context.Process` with the spawn context (line 105), so they are `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. That class subclasses `process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process` (`context.Process`), so the check is always False and `kill()` is never called. When a process is detected as `hang`, line 259 starts a second process for the same shards while the hung one keeps running. If the hung one recovers (for example a stalled Redis or Kafka call returns), both flush the same queues at once, which can produce duplicate or fragmented segments. Each hang leaks another process, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS. Fix: go back to calling `process.kill()` with the `ValueError` guard, and skip it only for `threading.Thread`, e.g. `if not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` or `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`. The same wrong check in `join` (line 346) means `terminate()` never runs there either. That one predates this PR.

join() skips terminate for the remaining processes once the deadline passes

Once the deadline has passed, `break` exits the loop before `process.terminate()` runs for the current process and every process after it. The old code always reached the terminate step after the wait. With several processes and a timeout, the first process's wait can use up the whole deadline, so the others are left running after `join` returns. They are daemons, so they only die when the parent exits. On a rebalance, though, a new flusher is created while these keep flushing their shards. Fix: replace `break` with skipping only the wait, and always try to terminate each remaining process (and fix the isinstance check noted at line 254 so terminate actually runs).

`spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` now caps each process, not the consumer

Each process gets its own `SpansBuffer(shards)`. `flush_segments` computes `max_segments_per_shard = ceil(max_flush_segments / len(self.assigned_shards))` from that buffer's own shards (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:382-384). The total flushed per cycle is therefore up to `num_processes × max-flush-segments`, where it used to be `max-flush-segments`. Kafka/Redis load grows when operators raise `--flusher-processes`. If this is intended, document the new meaning; if not, divide the option by `num_processes`.

Redis memory info is fetched once per process buffer, but each call covers the whole cluster

`get_memory_info` returns `iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client)` for the whole cluster, whatever the shards (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:375-376). Looping over `self.buffers` runs the same cluster-wide INFO query N times per `submit` and counts every node N times. The ratio stays correct because `used` and `available` are both multiplied by N, but the work is wasted. Calling it once, on any one buffer, is enough.

`time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op here because the test monkeypatches `time.sleep`

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, so `time.sleep(0.1)` returns immediately. The comment says it gives the flusher threads time to process. It doesn't, so `step.join()` still sets `stopped` right after the drift change. A thread that hasn't yet looped with the new drift exits without flushing, and `(msg,) = messages` fails intermittently. Either keep a reference to the real sleep before monkeypatching, or poll until `messages` is non-empty, with a timeout, before calling `join`.

`_create_process_for_shard` is never called

Nothing calls `_create_process_for_shard`. Restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly (line 259). Remove it.

Inconsistent metric tag key: `shards` here, `shard` elsewhere

`spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged `shards`, while `flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` (lines 185, 195) use `shard` for the same comma-joined value. Using one key makes dashboards consistent.

Docstring says one process per shard; the CLI default is one process total

The `--flusher-processes` CLI default is 1 (src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:434). Shards are spread round-robin over `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes (lines 60-66). Only a `None`/0 value from code paths that skip the CLI gives one process per shard. Reword it, e.g. 'Distributes shards across up to `max_processes` processes.'

Error IDs are zipped against nodestore results in the wrong order

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `get_multi` gives back one value per input id, in input order. It doesn't. `NodeStorage.get_multi` (src/sentry/nodestore/base.py:184) dedupes the ids. It builds the result from the uncached ids and then does `items.update(cache_items)` (base.py:199-205), so cached entries end up after the uncached ones. If only some events are cached, or an id repeats, each error gets another event's title, message and timestamp, and Seer summarises the wrong data with no sign anything is off. Fix: look up each event by its own key, e.g. `for event_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids): data = events.get(node_id)`.

Error timestamps (seconds) are compared with rrweb event timestamps (milliseconds)

`fetch_error_details` takes `data["timestamp"]` from the error event in nodestore, which is a float in epoch seconds. `gen_request_data` compares it with the top-level rrweb `event.get("timestamp")`, which is in epoch milliseconds (the breadcrumb payload carries its own seconds timestamp; see `event["data"]["payload"]["timestamp"]` in event_parser.py:312). So `error_ts < event_ts` is always true. Every error is emitted before the first breadcrumb, and the chronological merge this change adds never takes effect. Convert one side to the other's unit before comparing, e.g. `error["timestamp"] * 1000`.

Assemble analytics fires before the feature check

The `preprod_artifact.api.assemble` event is recorded before `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)`. Requests that end in a 403 still count as assembles. If the metric is meant to count real assemble attempts, record it after the feature gate.

Age/timestamp exclusivity checks use truthiness and accept reports with neither field

`self.initial_data.get("age")` is falsy when `age` is 0, which the Editor's Draft allows, so a report with both `age: 0` and `timestamp` passes. A report with neither field also validates, because both fields are `required=False` and each validator only runs when its own field is present. Checking `"age" in self.initial_data` and requiring exactly one of the two in `validate()` would match the comment's intent.

Hidden attributes still show when the search box is empty

`HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` is only checked inside the `.filter` on lines 65-69. When `searchQuery.trim()` is empty, the function returns `sorted` early on lines 61-63, so `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` still appear in the default view. They only disappear once the user types something. Apply the hidden-attribute filter to `sorted` before the early return, for example `const sorted = sortAttributes(attributes).filter(a => !HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(a.name));`.

Flex migration drops the gap and alignment the old FlexBox had

The old `FlexBox` set `align-items: center` and `gap: space(1)`, and `Container` added `justify-content: space-between` on top. `Flex` (static/app/components/core/layout/flex.tsx:18-26) only emits the props it is given. So the second placeholder group (`<Flex>` on line 27) now has no gap and no centering, and its three placeholders render touching each other. The main container on line 93 (`<Flex ref={setRef} justify="space-between">`) also loses `align-items: center` and `gap`, which shifts the tabs and vitals vertically. Add `align="center" gap={space(1)}` to both, as the first placeholder group on line 22 already does.

Waterfall container loses `height: 100%`

The removed `FlexBox` set `height: 100%` and `flex-grow: 1`. `<Flex direction="column" flex={1}>` sets neither a height nor anything equivalent (flex.tsx:18-26). If the parent is not a flex container along this axis, the waterfall no longer fills the available height. Check the trace page layout, or keep the height on a styled wrapper.

Is it intended that attribute keys stop filtering by environment?

Before this change the request sent `environment: selection.environments`. `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` now leaves it out ("environment left out intentionally as it's not supported"), and the query key no longer includes it, so changing the environment filter no longer refetches. The rewrite also drops `staleTime: 0`, `refetchOnWindowFocus: false` and `retry: false`, so the client defaults now apply. And `isLoading` now reports `isFetching`, so background refetches show as loading too. Did the endpoint ever honour `environment`, and are the retry and focus-refetch changes deliberate?

Custom renderer results of 0 or '' fall back to the default renderer

The prop docs and the story say only `undefined` triggers the fallback. But `if (cell)` (lines 32 and 71) also treats `0`, `''` and `null` as "not rendered". A custom renderer that returns `0` or an empty string is silently replaced by the default cell. Use `if (cell !== undefined)` to match the documented contract.

"Project not found" can flash while projects are still loading

`useProjectFromId` (static/app/utils/useProjectFromId.tsx:7-13) looks the id up in `useProjects().projects` and ignores the `fetching` state. If the projects store hasn't loaded yet, or the replay's project isn't in the user's loaded list yet, `project` is undefined and this branch shows a hard error instead of the loading indicator. Consider reading `fetching` from `useProjects()` and showing the error only after loading finishes.

Tests no longer send the `application/reports+json` content type that browsers use

Both success tests (`test_basic`, `test_handles_multiple_reports_both_specs`) used to post with `content_type="application/reports+json"`. Now they use the test client's default JSON format. The endpoint has a custom `BrowserReportsJSONParser` for that media type (src/sentry/issues/endpoints/browser_reporting_collector.py:63-82), and real browsers send it. After this change, no test covers that parser or the validation path reached through it. Keep at least one success case and one validation case on `application/reports+json`.

Recording event timestamps in seconds hide a seconds-vs-milliseconds mismatch in the error interleaving

The new tests give the rrweb event a top-level `timestamp` of `now.timestamp()`, which is in seconds (here and at line 254; `test_get_request_data` uses 1.5/2.0). In real recordings the top-level rrweb timestamp is in milliseconds, as the fixtures at `tests/sentry/replays/unit/test_event_parser.py:329` and `:363` show (`1674291701348`). `gen_request_data` (`src/sentry/replays/endpoints/project_replay_summarize_breadcrumbs.py:153-155`) compares the error's nodestore `timestamp` (seconds, from `fetch_error_details` at line 115) directly against `event.get("timestamp")`. With real millisecond data, every error is smaller than every event timestamp, so all errors get emitted before the first breadcrumb and the chronological ordering this feature promises silently fails. Because the tests use seconds on both sides, they pass and never catch it. Also, `test_get_with_error` only asserts `any(...)` membership, so it doesn't check ordering at all. Suggestion: build the segment events with millisecond timestamps, as real recordings have, and assert where the error line lands in `call_args["logs"]`. That test would fail until the endpoint normalizes the units.

Default audit-log path now crashes when the caller has no membership

`enable_advanced` is computed on every request, before `use_optimized` is checked. `organization_context.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` (src/sentry/organizations/services/organization/model.py:344-346). It is None whenever `request.user.id` has no membership: `convert_args` passes `user_id=request.user.id` (src/sentry/api/bases/organization.py:285-291), and that id is None for key-authenticated requests. For any such caller that isn't a superuser, `.has_global_access` raises AttributeError, so the endpoint returns 500 even when `optimized_pagination` is absent. Before this change, that request worked. Fix: check `use_optimized` first, and guard the member, e.g. `member = organization_context.member; enable_advanced = is_active_superuser(request) or (member is not None and member.has_global_access)`.

OptimizedCursorPaginator returns 500 for every non-empty audit-log page

The endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is `datetime`. `get_item_key` is copied from the integer `Paginator` and calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a `datetime`, which raises TypeError. `build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])` and `key(results[-1])` whenever there are results (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:121-137, 197). So `?optimized_pagination=true` returns 500 for any org that has audit entries.

`value_from_cursor` (line 843) has a related problem: it passes the raw millisecond integer into `build_queryset`, which compares it against a timestamp column (line 119-126). That breaks every cursor-based request too. `DateTimePaginator` converts in both places (lines 233-241). Subclass `DateTimePaginator` instead of `BasePaginator`, or reuse its key and value conversion.

Negative-offset branch cannot work: Django rejects negative QuerySet slices

`queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` in Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__`. So any cursor like `0:-5:0` sent by an admin with `optimized_pagination=true` returns 500. The comment's claim that "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. The same is true of the `else` branch at line 884 for prev cursors (`offset` is passed through unclamped).

The stated purpose, "access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", isn't a valid goal for a paginator either. If this were ever changed to slice a materialized list, the meaning of the cursor offset would silently change. Remove the branch and clamp the offset to >= 0 in every case, or reject a negative offset with a 400 when the cursor is parsed.

Gate uses `request.user.is_superuser` and `has_global_access`, so it doesn't mean "authorized administrators"

`request.user.is_superuser` is true even without an active superuser session. The permission class for this endpoint uses `is_active_superuser(request)` (src/sentry/api/bases/organization.py:124). Also, `OrganizationMember.has_global_access` defaults to True (src/sentry/models/organizationmember.py:216), so in practice the gate is open to almost any member who already passed the `org:write` check. Use `is_active_superuser(request)`. If admin-only access is really intended, check the role or scopes explicitly.

Comment in the shared BasePaginator is false

The comment says negative offsets are allowed and that "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions". The code clamps only non-prev cursors to 0. For prev cursors it still passes a negative offset to the QuerySet slice, and Django raises ValueError there. Clamping the forward path is a harmless improvement for all `Paginator`/`DateTimePaginator` users. Reword the comment to describe that, and clamp the prev path too, or reject negative offsets.

Comment describes behaviour the line doesn't implement

`self.offset = int(offset)` is unchanged and already accepted negative values. The new comment suggests a deliberate feature ("efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions") that doesn't exist; no paginator can slice with a negative offset. Remove the comment.

No tests for the new paginator or the new endpoint branch

The PR adds no tests. A single test of `GET` audit logs with `optimized_pagination=true` against an org with at least one entry would have caught the TypeError in `get_item_key`. A test with a member-less caller would have caught the AttributeError on the default path.

`get_result` duplicates BasePaginator.get_result almost verbatim

Apart from the negative-offset branch, which can't work, lines 845-911 repeat `BasePaginator.get_result` line for line. Once that branch is removed, the class adds nothing over `DateTimePaginator`, and the endpoint could keep using `DateTimePaginator` alone.

TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu while the new init log races with BuildIndex writes

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` (bleve.go:146) without taking `cacheMu`. This PR adds a call to it at search.go:216, which runs right after search.go:207-213 has started the goroutine that handles watch events. `handleEvent` → `getOrCreateIndex` → `BuildIndex` writes `b.cache[key]` (bleve.go:137-139), and that write holds `cacheMu`, which `TotalDocs` never takes. So a write event for a namespace/resource that has no index yet can land while `TotalDocs` is iterating. The Go runtime then aborts the process with `fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write`, and that cannot be recovered. The Prometheus collector (bleve_index_metrics.go:96) has the same race. This PR also narrows the `BuildIndex` lock so builds overlap. Fix: take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`/`RUnlock()` in `TotalDocs`, or copy the values under the lock before calling `DocCount`.

Parallel index build goroutines share `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`, so a build error can be lost

Every errgroup goroutine assigns to the outer `err` declared at search.go:181 (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and then returns it. They also increment `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronisation (line 189). Removing the `BuildIndex` mutex in bleve.go is meant to make these builds run in parallel (`WorkerThreads > 1`), which makes the interleaving likely. Goroutine A can set `err = X`, goroutine B can overwrite it with `nil`, and A then returns `nil`. `group.Wait()` reports success, init logs 'search index initialized', and nothing records that A's index failed to build. The span attribute count is also racy. Fix: use a goroutine-local `_, _, err := s.build(...)` and an `atomic.Int64` (or a mutex) for the counter.

Eager Init in the constructor makes every in-process caller connect to the DB and build all indexes before the constructor returns

`Init` used to run lazily on the first request. It now runs inside `NewResourceServer`, so it runs `lifecycle.Init` (the resource DB connect and ping, sql/backend.go:93-106), the whole `search.init` index build and `initWatcher` before the constructor returns. For the in-process path (unified/client.go:101), that work now happens during dependency construction and blocks Grafana startup. A resource-DB or indexing failure now fails startup, where before it only failed unified-storage requests. Is that intended for every deployment that wires this client, including ones that never serve unified storage? Two related details: on failure, `s.cancel` is never called. And if `initWatcher` fails after `search.init` succeeded, the search watch goroutine (search.go:202-213, on `context.Background()`) keeps running for a server that was never returned.

After Stop, requests are no longer rejected

`Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to 'service is stopping'/'service is stopped' (server.go:321, 339). That only worked because every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned the stored error. With those calls removed (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, blob, IsHealthy), `initErr` is written and never read after construction. A Create/Update/Delete that arrives after `Stop` now succeeds against the backend, even though `s.cancel()` has already stopped the watcher. `IsHealthy` also keeps reporting the backend's status instead of an error. Either keep a cheap `initErr` check in the handlers or drop the dead assignments in `Stop`.

Postgres skip removes coverage of the storage-server target with no tracking issue

This is the only integration test that starts the `StorageServer` module. Skipping it on postgres leaves that target untested on that database. The same PR makes `service.start` block on `NewResourceServer` → `Init` (DB connect plus full index build). Is the Drone failure caused by this change, for example startup no longer fitting in the 500 ms sleep at line 56? If it is, the skip hides a regression. If it isn't, could the TODO link an issue?

MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass` in its body. It inherits five abstract members and implements none of them: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (`src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py:142-170`), plus `evaluate` from the base class. `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (`src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86`), so any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` there.

That exception comes up through `process_detectors` (`processors/detector.py:53`), which has no try/except. So it also stops evaluation and the state commit for every other detector later in the same batch. Before this change the handler built fine and returned `[]`. Nothing in `src/` calls `process_detectors` yet, so this won't break today, but the type is registered and wired in. Two ways to fix it: keep it on a concrete base until it's implemented, or add stub implementations (for example `counter_names = []` and methods that raise `NotImplementedError` or return empty values). The `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector` comment on line 10 is also out of date now.

Occurrence assertions only compare the hardcoded id, so wrong group_key/value/priority still pass

`IssueOccurrence.__eq__` compares only `id` (`src/sentry/issues/issue_occurrence.py:181-184`), and `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` always uses the same `id` (line 252). So every `result=occurrence` check in these tests passes whatever `fingerprint`, `type` or `initial_issue_priority` the hook produced. The tests already show the gap. Here the expected occurrence is built for `"val1"` while the code under test evaluates `"group_key"`, so the fingerprints differ (`<id>:val1` vs `<id>:group_key`) and the test still passes. In the same way, the expected values are built with `6` while the evaluated values are `10` (lines 190 and 549) and `100` (line 489).

The new hook's real contract is that `evaluate_group_key_value` passes the right `group_key`, `value` and `PriorityLevel(new_status)` to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. No test checks that: passing the wrong group key or priority to the hook would go unnoticed. Two fixes: build the expected occurrence with the same arguments as the code under test, and add a check that matters. For example, assert on `result.result.fingerprint` and `initial_issue_priority`, or wrap `build_occurrence_and_event_data` in a mock and use `assert_called_once_with(group_key, value, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`.

evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

`evaluate` now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the docstring still says "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". Update it to say it returns a dict keyed by group key.

Monitor context sends the raw config, not the copy with the readable schedule_type

`get_monitor_environment_context` copies the config and swaps `schedule_type` for its display value (lines 160-162). Line 168 then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config`, the original, so the copy is thrown away and the event's monitor context still holds the integer `schedule_type`. This bug was already in `mark_failed.py` and was moved here unchanged. Since this PR is reorganizing the code anyway, consider returning `config` here, which is what `MonitorSerializer.serialize` does at src/sentry/monitors/serializers.py:240-242. Any test that asserts the current context shape would need updating.

get_failure_reason docstring has typos and examples the function cannot produce

The moved docstring says "humam readible". Its examples don't match the code either. The plural branch returns "... check-ins detected" (line 156), never "... were detected", and builds parts like "2 missed" rather than "2 missed check-ins". The singular branch uses `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP`, which has no "A failed check-in was detected" entry. Consider fixing the docstring now that the function lives in its own module.

`queued` default is computed once at import time, not per instance

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs a single time, when the class body runs at module import. Every `AssignmentSource` the process builds afterwards, including every one from `from_integration` (line 22), gets the worker's start-up timestamp rather than the time the assignment was queued. Nothing reads `queued` yet (no matches under `src/sentry/integrations`), so for now the wrong value travels silently through the task kwargs. Any later use, such as ordering or staleness checks, would get a wrong answer and nothing would report it. Fix: `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The new `test_to_dict` (tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:36) only asserts `queued is not None`, so it can't catch this. Asserting that two instances made at different times differ, or using a frozen clock, would.

No test that a different source integration still syncs outbound, or that deassign honours the source

The new test covers only the case where the source matches the single linked integration, and checks that `sync_assignee_outbound` is not called. The other half of the stated contract has no test: per the comment at src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:387-389, other integrations should still propagate changes outward. A test with a second integration as `assignment_source`, asserting the call still happens with that `assignment_source`, would cover it. The deassign path that now forwards `assignment_source` (src/sentry/models/groupassignee.py:238-240), used by `sync_group_assignee_inbound` with `assign=False`, also has no test with a matching source.

`assignment_source` added to abstract `sync_status_outbound` but nothing passes it

The abstract signature gains `assignment_source`, but no caller in this change passes it, and no status-sync path builds an `AssignmentSource`. The parameter only advertises loop prevention for status sync that doesn't exist. Either wire it through the status sync path, or leave the signature alone until that work lands.

Closing a strategy shuts down the factory's shared pool; after the first rebalance every message is dropped and its offset committed

The factory builds one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` (result_consumer.py:131-137), and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands that same pool to every new strategy (result_consumer.py:254-259). On a rebalance Arroyo closes the old strategy and calls `create_with_partitions` again. `close()` (and `join()`, which calls `close()` again at 344-345) runs `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `q.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers (231-243). The next strategy gets the same pool with dead workers and shut-down queues. In `FixedQueuePool.submit`, `work_queue.put` now raises `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches it as a generic `Exception` (317-325) and marks the offset complete, so the commit loop commits it. From the first rebalance on, every uptime result is thrown away and committed, and the only trace is one `logger.exception` per message.

The shared `OffsetTracker` has a second problem: it keeps entries for partitions that were revoked. Those can end up in the `committable` dict passed to `commit` for partitions this consumer no longer owns.

Fix: give each strategy its own pool and tracker (create them in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`), or don't let the strategy shut down a pool it does not own. Add a test that calls `create_with_partitions` twice with a `close()` in between.

Arroyo's `commit` callback is called from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread (270-271) and calls `commit_function`, which calls Arroyo's `Commit` (result_consumer.py:249-252). That callback stages offsets on the consumer and may commit them. Arroyo expects it to be called from the processing thread, inside `submit`/`poll`, while the main thread is polling the same consumer. Every other mode in this factory commits through `CommitOffsets` on the main thread (result_consumer.py:214-242). Suggested fix: have the worker threads only update the tracker, and call `commit` from `poll()` on the main thread. I could not read Arroyo's source in this checkout to confirm its thread-safety contract, so the race itself is unconfirmed.

Queues are unbounded: no backpressure, despite the docstring

`queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`, and `poll()` only emits a gauge. If the workers fall behind (slow DB or Redis), the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and stores every message in memory until the process is OOM-killed. The docstring at 253 promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which this code does not do. Bound the queues and raise `MessageRejected` from `submit` when a target queue is full (or when `total_items` passes a limit).

`join(timeout)` ignores its timeout and can block for about 2×(5 + 5·N) seconds

`join` ignores `timeout` and calls `close()` again. `close()` waits up to 5 s for the commit thread, then `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker one after another with 5 s each (242-243). With the default 20 queues and a stuck `result_processor`, one call can take 105 s. Arroyo calls `close()` and then `join()`, so a rebalance can block for longer than that, which can exceed `max.poll.interval.ms`. Nothing bounds the total wait. Suggestion: honour `timeout` as one overall deadline and make `join` a no-op after the first close. Separately, items processed after the commit thread's last pass are never committed, so they are reprocessed after a rebalance.

Commits stop for good if the partition has a gap in offset numbers

`get_committable_offsets` walks every integer from `start` up and stops at the first number that isn't in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not always contiguous: transactional control records and compaction leave gaps. One gap would stop commits on that partition forever, with no error. Instead, walk the sorted offsets this consumer has actually seen: the committable offset is the one just before the lowest offset still outstanding.

`test_preserves_order_within_group` does not check order

The test only asserts `len(self.processed_results) == 5`. It would still pass if the five messages were processed in any order. Assert the sequence of processed offsets or payloads instead. The two `test_concurrent_processing_*` tests have the same gap: they only count items and never show that two groups ran at the same time. No test covers a strategy being closed and recreated against the same factory, which is how the pool-shutdown blocker above happens.

Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring, and only passes because of timing

The docstring says errors "don't block offset commits for other messages". The assertion checks the reverse: `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, meaning nothing was committed.

What the code actually does: the worker's `finally` calls `complete_offset` even when the processor raises (`queue_consumer.py:148-149`). So offsets 100 and 101 both finish, and `_commit_loop` commits `{partition: 102}` on its first tick, 1s after the strategy is created (`queue_consumer.py:276-287`, `+1` at `result_consumer.py:251`).

The test only passes because the wait loop exits about 0.3s after both calls (`time.sleep(0.2); break`), before that first tick. On a slow CI runner the tick lands first, `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`, and the test fails. Also, as written it would never catch a regression where a failing message blocks commits.

Fix: wait for a commit, like `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit` does (`len(committed_offsets) > 0`), then assert `committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`.

Graceful-shutdown test only checks an attribute that is always cleared

`assert factory.queue_pool is None` always passes: `shutdown()` sets `self.queue_pool = None` no matter what happened to the workers (`result_consumer.py:183-185`). Nothing checks that the 5 queued results were drained before the workers stopped, which is what "graceful" means for `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` (`queue_consumer.py:231-243`, `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` plus `join(timeout=5.0)`).

Unlike every sibling test, this one doesn't patch `type(factory.result_processor).__call__`. So the real uptime processor runs on worker threads, outside the test's DB connection and outside the `self.feature(...)` block used in `send_result`. Suggestion: patch `__call__` and assert `call_count == 5` after `factory.shutdown()`.

Concurrent-subscriptions test doesn't check concurrency

The test claims different subscriptions run concurrently, but it only asserts `call_count == 2`, which serial processing on a single queue would also satisfy. With `max_workers=2`, queues are picked by `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` (`queue_consumer.py:202`), so the two subscriptions can hash to the same queue, depending on random UUIDs and hash randomization.

To actually test it, either assert that the two keys map to different queue indexes, or have the mocked processor block on an event and check that both calls are in flight at once.

Strategy commit threads are never stopped in the unit tests

Every `create_with_partitions` call in thread-queue-parallel mode starts a daemon `_commit_loop` thread (`queue_consumer.py:270-271`). That thread only stops in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` (`queue_consumer.py:335-342`).

The new tests call `factory.shutdown()`, which stops the queue workers, but never `consumer.close()`. Each test therefore leaves a thread polling `get_committable_offsets` and calling the test's commit callback every second for the rest of the pytest session.

Calling `consumer.close()` (or `terminate()`) before `factory.shutdown()` would match how arroyo tears a strategy down.

Should an offset gap stop commits for good?

This test locks in that once an offset is missing, the consumer never commits past it. `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets` (`queue_consumer.py:89-93`). Offsets 102 and 103 stay uncommitted forever, even after they are processed.

Real Kafka partitions can have offset gaps, for example from transactional control records or log compaction. On such a topic the consumer group's committed offset would freeze at the gap, and everything after it would be re-processed on every rebalance or restart.

Can the uptime-results topic ever have such gaps? If it can, the test should expect commits to move past offsets that were never delivered, instead of asserting `<= 101`.

OptimizedCursorPaginator breaks on the datetime key it is used with

The audit log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"` (organization_auditlogs.py:79-80). `get_item_key` copies `Paginator.get_item_key`, so it calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a `datetime` and raises `TypeError`. That happens inside `build_cursor` (cursors.py:258-265) for any page that has results. `value_from_cursor` hands back the raw integer cursor value, and `build_queryset` puts it straight into `datetime <= %s` (paginator.py:119-126), so a follow-up cursor builds an invalid timestamp-vs-integer comparison. Result: any superuser or global-access member who sends `?optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500. If this paginator stays, it needs `DateTimePaginator`'s key and cursor conversion (paginator.py:230-241), for example by subclassing `DateTimePaginator`.

The 'negative offset' feature can only fail, and the comments claim otherwise

`Cursor.from_string` accepts a negative offset (cursors.py:59). This branch then runs `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` with it. Django QuerySets reject negative indexing with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so the request ends in a 500. The comments say Django 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that this 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds… safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. The first is false. The second describes a bypass of pagination bounds as the intended behaviour. Remove the branch and clamp `start_offset` to 0. A negative cursor offset should be a 400, not something the paginator tries to honour.

`organization_context.member` can be None, so the audit log endpoint can now 500 for every request

`RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` (organizations/services/organization/model.py:346). `enable_advanced` is computed on every request, not only when `optimized_pagination=true` is set. So any caller that passes `OrganizationAuditPermission` without a membership and without `user.is_superuser` now gets `AttributeError` before pagination runs. Examples are a legacy API key with `org:write`, where `request.user` is anonymous. Before this change, these callers got the normal audit log. Compute the flag only inside the `use_optimized` branch, and guard `member is not None`.

Gate uses `user.is_superuser` instead of `is_active_superuser(request)`

Elsewhere this codebase checks superuser privilege with `is_active_superuser(request)`, which requires an active superuser session; see OrganizationAuditPermission at api/bases/organization.py:124. `request.user.is_superuser` is true for a superuser account even without an elevated session. The path it unlocks is currently broken (see the other findings). Still, if it is kept, gate it the same way as the permission class.

BasePaginator comment says negative offsets are allowed and safe

Every paginator subclass shares this change. For `is_prev` cursors, a negative offset still goes into `queryset[offset:stop]`, and Django raises `ValueError`, the same as before this change. Only next-page cursors get clamped. The comment ('allow negative offsets… the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') describes behaviour that does not exist. Either clamp both directions or drop the comment. The same goes for the comment added at utils/cursors.py:26-27.

Switching segment keys from SET to ZSET has no migration for keys already in Redis

Segment keys `span-buf:s:*` that the old code wrote are SETs, and they live up to `redis_ttl` (3600 s, buffer.py:151). After deploy, `ZADD` (buffer.py:197), `ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE` here, and `ZSCAN` in `_load_segment_data` (buffer.py:434) all fail with WRONGTYPE on those keys. The pipeline raises, so `process_batch`/the flusher fail repeatedly until the old keys expire. While old and new consumers run side by side, the old code's `SADD`/`SSCAN` hit the new ZSETs the same way. Use a new key prefix, or handle the WRONGTYPE case.

Spans over 1000 are dropped silently, and `max_segment_spans` is now dead

Before, an oversized segment was skipped with a metric and an error log (`segment_span_count_exceeded`, now removed from buffer.py:449). Now `ZPOPMIN` discards the earliest-ending spans with no metric, no log, and nothing in the script's return value. The 1000 is hardcoded, while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (buffer.py:150,158) is still accepted but read nowhere. Pass the limit as an ARGV, return the evicted count, and emit a metric in `process_spans`.

ZUNIONSTORE sums the scores of duplicate members

`ZUNIONSTORE` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload ends up in both keys, for example a redelivered Kafka message, its score becomes the sum of two end timestamps. That puts it at the top of the ranking, so the eviction at lines 62-63 never removes it. Add `AGGREGATE MAX` to both calls (lines 47 and 53).

Redirect depth limit cut 10x and its explanation removed

The loop limit drops from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining the consequence ('segment trees of depth N may not be joined together correctly') is deleted. The PR body does not mention the change. Keep the comment, with the new number.

No test covers the new eviction or the new paginator

The test changes only add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0` to existing fixtures, with the same value everywhere. Nothing covers the 1000-span cap, which spans `ZPOPMIN` evicts (ordered by end timestamp), merges across keys, or `OptimizedCursorPaginator`/`optimized_pagination`. A test of any of these would have caught the datetime `TypeError`.

Negated event.type:error queries are treated as error queries

`_is_error_focused_query` does a plain substring check, `"event.type:error" in query`. So `!event.type:error` (meaning "everything except errors") and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both count as error-focused. For the discover dataset on allowlisted projects, `count()` then becomes `upsampled_count()`, i.e. `sum(sample_weight)`, over non-error rows. That count is wrong (or fails, if the column isn't there), and no error says why. Parse the query, or at least reject a match preceded by `!` and any query with OR/other event.type terms. Add a test for the negated case.

sum(sample_weight) undercounts events without sample_weight

`upsampled_count` is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and has no null fallback. The comment says the schema guarantees `sample_weight` for every event in an allowlisted project. Nothing in this repo enforces that, though: events stored before a project joined the allowlist, and events sent without `contexts.error_sampling`, have no weight (the test factory only sets `sample_rate` when `client_sample_rate` is present, `src/sentry/testutils/factories.py:353`). `sum` ignores NULLs, so those events add 0, and charts silently show fewer errors than really happened. Use `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`. Add a test that mixes events with and without `error_sampling`.

Caching the allowlist check adds a round trip and staleness for no gain

`options.get` already comes from the options store's local cache. Wrapping it in `cache.get`/`cache.set` adds a network round trip to the shared cache on every events-stats request. It also keeps results up to 60s stale after an allowlist change. Nothing calls `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (line 67), so the docstring's "should be called when the allowlist changes" never happens. The docstring of `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` (lines 50-53) says the allowlist is read fresh each time "intentionally", which contradicts this cache. Consider dropping the cache and the unused invalidation helper, or wiring the helper up. The cached path in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` also has no test.

Upsampling decision ignores scoped_dataset and the query actually run

The check passes the outer `dataset` and reads `request.GET["query"]`. It doesn't look at the `scoped_dataset` and `query` that `_get_event_stats` receives. In the dashboard-widget split path (lines 362-394), `_get_event_stats` runs against `discover` with `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction` while `dataset` is metrics-enhanced. The check then always returns False, so error widgets split this way never get upsampled counts. Base the decision on `scoped_dataset` and the `query` argument.

Top-N groups are ranked by raw count but charted by upsampled count

For top events, only `timeseries_columns` are transformed. `selected_columns` and `orderby` (e.g. `-count()`) stay unchanged, so the top groups are picked by raw `count()` while their series show `upsampled_count()`. Projects with different client sample rates can end up ranked in a different order from the values plotted. Consider transforming the field list too, or document the difference.

Stray gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d29...`) at `sentry-repo`, and the repository has no `.gitmodules`. This looks like a nested checkout committed by accident. It isn't part of the feature, and it breaks `git submodule` tooling and clones that recurse into submodules. Remove it from the PR.

Test creates Organization directly instead of using self.create_organization

CLAUDE.md (Common Gotchas #7) says to "Use `self.create_*` helpers, not direct model creation". Replace `Organization.objects.create(name="test-org")` with `self.create_organization(name="test-org")`.

Comments contradict the asserted upsampled values

The comments say "First bucket has 1 event" and "Second bucket has 1 event", but the asserts expect 10 (the upsampled count). Reword them, e.g. "1 event at sample rate 0.1, upsampled to 10". There's also no test for the top-events path, the negated `event.type:error` case, or events without `error_sampling` context.

Denial cache key is ambiguous: different (name, folder) pairs map to the same key

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins `name` and `parent` with `_`, and dashboard/folder UIDs may themselves contain `_`. A denial for dashboard `a` in folder `b_c` produces `ns.perm_<uid>_dashboards:read_a_b_c`, the same key as dashboard `a_b` in folder `c`. Check reads the denial cache first (`service.go:116-121`) and returns `Allowed: false` without looking at permissions, so the second dashboard is silently denied for up to `shortCacheTTL` even when the user can access it. The key also leaves out the identity type (`checkReq.IdentityType`). Subjects of different types that share a UID string (for example the anonymous or renderer subject and a user) share denial entries, even though `getIdentityPermissions` resolves their permissions differently (`service.go:330-339`). Fix: use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode the fields (length-prefix or escape them), and add the identity type to the key.

Every first-time denial now runs a full permission DB query

`getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions` no longer read `permCache` (`service.go:379-380`, `423-424`). So whenever the cached scope map doesn't grant a resource, Check calls `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` again (`service.go:400`). Only that one exact `(user, action, name, folder)` tuple then goes into the denial cache. Before this change, one DB query per user/action every 30s served every Check, allowed or denied. Now a caller that checks many distinct resources the user can't see (search/list filtering by per-item Check) triggers one permission query per resource. Singleflight only merges calls that run at the same time. You could re-fetch only when the cached entry is older than some threshold, or keep the read-through and invalidate the cache on grant instead.

"explicit cache deny" test passes even without the denial cache

The comment says the permission cache is set up to *allow* access "to prove this is not checked", but the map value is `false`. So `scopeMap["dashboards:uid:dash1"]` is false and the cached path denies anyway. The DB fallback then uses the default empty `fakeStore` from `setupService` (`service_test.go:1328,1340-1342`), which also denies. The assertion `assert.False(resp.Allowed)` would pass with the denial-cache lookup removed. Set the value to `true` (and/or give the store an allowing permission) so the test fails unless the denial entry short-circuits.

`NoopCache` is exported from the `authz` package but only used internally

`NoopCache` is used only by `ProvideAuthZClient` (line 103). Exporting it adds public API to `pkg/services/authz`. Make it unexported (`noopCache`), and consider adding `var _ cache.Cache = (*noopCache)(nil)` so the interface conformance is checked at compile time.

OAuth `state` is a constant, so it gives no CSRF protection

`state = pipeline.signature`, and `signature` is `md5_text(*pipe_ids)` over the view class names (src/sentry/pipeline/base.py:132-133). Every user and every session gets the same value; the tests hardcode `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`. The check at line 412 therefore can't tell a callback this session started from a forged one. An attacker can send someone who is mid-pipeline to `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker's code>&state=9cae…`. That binds `github_authenticated_user` to the attacker's GitHub login (login CSRF), and the new sender check exists to protect exactly that value. Fix: generate a random per-pipeline nonce, `bind_state` it before the redirect, and compare it with `constant_time_compare` on return.

`metadata["sender"]` raises KeyError for integrations created through the Sentry pipeline

`build_integration` only writes `metadata["sender"]` when the state has a sender (lines 376-377). The webhook passes one (webhook.py:204-207), but the pipeline state doesn't, and `test_basic_flow` confirms metadata without `sender` (test_integration.py:303-310). Deleting an OrganizationIntegration does not delete the Integration (deletions/defaults/organizationintegration.py). So a user who installed through Sentry, uninstalled, and then reinstalls (into the same or another org) reaches this line with an existing Integration, no OrganizationIntegration and no `sender`. The result is an unhandled KeyError (500) instead of an error page. `installation.py:44` already guards this with `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`. Handle the missing key explicitly: render `error(...)`, or decide what should be allowed.

Network failures or GitHub errors in the OAuth exchange give a 500, not the error dialog

`safe_urlopen(...)` runs outside the `try`, so a connection error or timeout escapes. `get_user_info` (identity/github/provider.py:7-17) calls `resp.raise_for_status()` and `resp.json()` with no handling, so a 401 from `/user` (expired or revoked token) or a non-JSON body also escapes. Every other failure in this view renders `github-integration-failed.html`, which posts `success: false` to the opener window. These paths instead leave the popup on a 500 page and the opener never gets a message. Put both calls inside the `try` and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

The installer check is skipped whenever the Integration row doesn't exist yet

The new sender comparison only runs when an Integration already exists. If the `installation` webhook hasn't arrived yet (or failed), the code goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()`. `build_integration` then attaches any `installation_id` it is given to the current org, whoever the authenticated GitHub user is. The guard against linking someone else's installation therefore depends on webhook timing. Consider verifying access with the user token you already have, e.g. `GET /user/installations`, and checking that `installation_id` is in the list. That works whether or not the row exists.

Authorize URL is built by string formatting with no encoding

`redirect_uri` is an absolute URL containing `:` and `/` (and possibly a query on some deployments), and it goes into the query string unencoded. GitHub tolerates this today, as the test shows, but `urlencode({...})` is the safe way to build the query and is what `OAuth2LoginView` does.

`test_installation_not_found` no longer tests a missing installation

The test now sends `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which doesn't match the pipeline signature. It fails at the state check (integration.py:412) with "Invalid installation request." and never reaches `build_integration`. That leaves the 404 branch that raises "The GitHub installation could not be found." (integration.py:354-356) untested, while the test name still claims to cover it. Use the real state so the flow gets to the installation lookup, and keep the original assertion.

No tests for the new OAuth failure paths or a successful sender match

Nothing tests a token exchange that returns no `access_token`, a `/user` response without `login`, or a reinstall where the existing Integration's `sender.login` matches the authenticated user (the success case of the new check). `test_github_user_mismatch` only covers the mismatch. Adding these would have caught the KeyError and the 500 paths reported above.

Update-time login invalidation checks the org-wrapped `isEnabled`, which the cached query never looks at

`update()` gets `original` from `getById(...)` (line 91). That returns `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...)` (line 141), and for an IdP linked to a disabled organization its `isEnabled()` is `false` (lines 438-441). The list this code caches comes from the JPA `getAllStream` query (`IdentityProviderStorageProvider.java:165-184`). That query filters only on DB columns (enabled, linkOnly, hideOnLogin, orgId, BROKER_PUBLIC) and ignores whether the organization is enabled.

So here is what happens. An org IdP is in the cached `ALL`/`ORG_ONLY` lists. The admin disables the organization, then sets `hideOnLogin=true` (or `linkOnly=true`, or removes `BROKER_PUBLIC`) on that IdP. `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is `false` because the org is disabled, and `test(updated)` is also `false`, so the early return at line 405 skips the invalidation. The cached query keeps the IdP's id. When the organization is enabled again, nothing invalidates the login keys either. `getForLogin` then returns the IdP through `getById`. `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` re-checks only `isEnabled()` (lines 75 and 80), so the hidden, link-only or non-public IdP appears on the login page with no error. It stays there until something else invalidates the key.

Fix: evaluate the predicate on the unwrapped stored model, e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(model.getInternalId())`, or test the raw fields, so the check matches what the cached query selects.

Cleanup removes the alias "alias" instead of the IdPs the test created

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` targets a literal `"alias"`, not `"idp-alias-" + i`. Line 425 has the same mistake for `idp-alias-20`. None of the 20 IdPs created here are cleaned up, and each cleanup call targets a provider that doesn't exist. Use `get(idpRep.getAlias())`, captured before the call.

enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature-flag lookup does nothing

Both branches return `false`, so the `IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` call (line 195) has no effect, and the inverted `enabled := !...` makes it look like the flag is honoured when it is not. Someone who turns on `sqlExpressions` would expect it to do something. If the goal is to switch SQL expressions off for everyone, delete the helper and return the error directly in the `QueryTypeSQL` case, with a comment saying why (DuckDB was removed). If it is meant to depend on the flag, it should be `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`. As written, the helper's name and body say different things.

Legacy parse path tells users their SQL is invalid instead of saying SQL expressions are disabled

Only `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` got the new gate, and it only runs when `FlagExpressionParser` is on (`pkg/expr/nodes.go:123`). By default, a `sql` expression goes through `nodes.go:159-160` → `UnmarshalSQLCommand` → `NewSQLCommand` → `sql.TablesList`. That now always fails, because the stub `RunCommands` returns "not implemented" (`pkg/expr/sql/db.go:16-17`, `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:26-30`). The user then gets the BadRequest `sql-invalid-sql` with the public message "error reading SQL command", which reads as a problem with their query. Each request also logs at Error level in `parser.go:28` and Warn level here. Gating `NewSQLCommand` itself (or `UnmarshalSQLCommand`) with an explicit "SQL expressions are not supported" error would give both paths the same clear message.

No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock

This is check-then-lock without a second check. Several requests can see a nil cache on the RLock fast path at the same time, for example the first page loads after startup. Each one then waits for the write lock and reads and parses `assets-manifest.json` again, one after another (lines 59-69), even though the first one has already filled `entryPointAssetsCache`. The result is still correct, but this is the duplicate work the cache is there to avoid, and the requests queue behind each other.

Suggested fix: after `Lock()`, check again with `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. You could also use `sync.Once`/`singleflight` for the non-Dev path.

No concurrent test for the new locking

The PR exists to remove a data race on `entryPointAssetsCache`, but no test calls `GetWebAssets` from several goroutines at once. Without one, `go test -race` can't catch the race if it comes back. A small test would cover it: start N goroutines calling `GetWebAssets` against the testdata manifest and check that they all get the same non-nil pointer. I only read `webassets_test.go` through the grep match at line 50, so I haven't confirmed that no such test exists elsewhere.

Debug logging left in at Error level, with every ID in the batch

Six `r.log.Error(...)` calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) run on every batch of every cleanup cycle, including successful ones and empty batches. Each call logs the full `ids` slice: 100 IDs at the default `cleanupjob_batchsize` (pkg/setting/setting.go:710), and up to tens of thousands for large batch sizes. They also log `err`, which is always nil on lines 534/554/576 because the error was already returned above. Error-level output fires alerting and floods logs while nothing is wrong. Remove these calls, or turn them into one `Debug` line per run with counts only.

Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

This looks like a leftover from local testing. The ticker drives every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history; lines 96-105), so they now run 10× as often. The 9-minute timeout at line 89 was sized to fit inside the 10-minute interval. With a 1-minute ticker, a long run is followed straight away by another, so cleanup runs almost continuously. That works against a PR titled "Database Performance Optimizations". Restore `time.Minute * 10`.

Quadratic string building for inlined SQLite IDs

`values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the whole string built so far on every iteration, so the cost is O(n²) in the batch size. This branch only runs when the batch size is above 999. At the 32767 batch size the new test uses, that is roughly 32767²/2 × ~7 bytes ≈ several GB of copying per DELETE, repeated for every batch and for the tag cleanup too. Build the list with `strings.Builder` or with `strconv.FormatInt` plus `strings.Join`.

Placeholder count is unbounded on MySQL/Postgres

On every driver except SQLite with batch size > 999, the DELETE gets one `?` per ID. PostgreSQL and MySQL prepared statements both cap bound parameters at 65535. So with `cleanupjob_batchsize` set above 65535, every batch now fails and annotation cleanup stops entirely: the error is returned from `CleanAnnotations` and only logged by `cleanUpOldAnnotations` (pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go:126-127). The old single-statement subquery had no such limit. Either cap the chunk size used in `deleteByIDs`, or inline the integer IDs for these drivers too (as the SQLite branch does).

Test case no longer runs the delete "again"

Each subtest now creates fresh data and wipes it in `t.Cleanup`. This case therefore no longer re-runs the max-count cleanup on state the previous case left behind; it just creates 9 annotations (3 per type) with MaxCount 3. It is still a valid check, but the name now describes a scenario that isn't tested. Either rename it, or run `cleaner.Run` twice inside one subtest to keep the idempotency check.

Cleanup registered after the setup assertions

`t.Cleanup` is registered only after `createTestAnnotations` and the two count assertions have passed. If any of them fails via `require` (FailNow), the rows already inserted stay in the shared `fakeSQL`. Every later subtest then fails on its initial count assertion, which hides the real failure. Register the cleanup before inserting.

Background legacy writes use the request context, which is cancelled once the response is sent

Create (L50-57), Delete (L108-114), Update (L134-141) and DeleteCollection (L161-167) now run the legacy write in a goroutine and return right away. Each goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, and `ctx` is the incoming request context. net/http cancels that context when the handler returns, and here the handler returns right after the goroutine starts. So the legacy SQL write (e.g. `pkg/registry/apis/playlist/legacy_storage.go:115`, `:160`) races against cancellation and can be aborted. The 10s timeout is only an upper bound, so it doesn't prevent this.

Nothing reports the failure. The goroutines only call `recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...)` and never log the error; before this change the legacy error was logged (`log...Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`). Mode 3 reads only from unified storage, so users won't notice, but legacy storage silently falls behind. That matters as soon as someone goes back to mode 1/2, because those modes read from legacy.

Suggested fix: derive the goroutine's context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, which keeps request values such as namespace and identity that legacy storage needs (`request.NamespaceInfoFrom`, legacy_storage.go:102,136), then add the timeout, and log `errObjectSt`/`err`. Mode 1 uses the same pattern for its background storage writes (`dualwriter_mode1.go:54`).

Duration metrics recorded on the wrong histogram or with the wrong label

Several durations are recorded under the wrong store or label, so the dual-writer dashboards show wrong numbers and nothing signals it:
- L45 (Create) and L129 (Update) record a failed **Storage** call with `recordLegacyDuration`, so storage errors appear as legacy errors.
- L166 (DeleteCollection) records the **Legacy** call with `recordStorageDuration`, so legacy timings are mixed into the storage histogram.
- L106 (Delete) passes `name` where the `kind` label goes (`recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...)`). This puts the wrong value in that label and creates a new label series for every deleted object, which is a cardinality problem.

Fix: use `recordStorageDuration` at L45/L129, `recordLegacyDuration` at L166, and `options.Kind` at L106.

Delete puts `d.Log` into the context instead of the enriched `log`

The other methods call `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`. Delete passes `d.Log`, so storage and legacy code reading the logger from the context lose the `name`/`kind`/`method` values. Use `log` here.

Delete no longer cleans up legacy when the object is missing from unified storage

The old code treated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from Storage.Delete as non-fatal and still deleted from legacy. Now any storage error, NotFound included, returns before the legacy delete. If an object exists in legacy but not in unified storage (e.g. a mode 3 legacy create that failed or was cancelled, see the context finding), a delete can never remove it from legacy. Was dropping that tolerance intended?

Legacy update re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object unified storage stored

The old code wrapped the result of Storage.Update in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so legacy received exactly the object that was stored. Mode 2 still does this (`dualwriter_mode2.go:298`). Now `objInfo` is passed through unchanged, and the playlist legacy store calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old)` against its own row (`legacy_storage.go:142-147`). For a PATCH or an admission-mutating update, the patch and admission run a second time against a possibly different base object, so the two stores can diverge. Consider passing `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}`.

Mode 3 tests never check that the legacy write happens

Legacy and storage share one `mock.Mock` (`legacyStoreMock{m, l}`, `storageMock{m, s}`), and the legacy call runs in a goroutine that may still be running after the test ends. As a result no test asserts that `Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection` is called, or with what arguments. Test names like "creating an object only in the unified store" describe behaviour the code doesn't have (it also writes to legacy). In the error case (L37-44) the storage failure is configured through `setupLegacyFn`, which only works because the mock is shared. Consider separate mocks for each store and a wait on the legacy call (e.g. `assert.Eventually` on `AssertCalled`) so the async write is covered.

"Silence notifications" does nothing in the new list view

In the list view, `GrafanaRuleListItem` now passes only `promRule` (GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx:47), so `rule` is undefined here. `AlertRuleMenu` still shows the Silence item, because `canSilence` is true through `grafanaSilenceAbility` (AlertRuleMenu.tsx:96, 126-132). Fix: open the drawer from the prom rule when the ruler rule is missing (or pass the rule UID to the drawer), or hide the item until the drawer can open.

Pause and Delete are gone from the Grafana rule list menu even when the user has permission

This PR computes `canPause` and `canDelete` from the prom-rule abilities (lines 83, 87). The menu items, though, still need a ruler rule: Pause needs `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123) and Delete needs `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165). The list view no longer has a ruler rule (GrafanaRuleListItem.tsx:47 passes only `promRule`), so both items disappear for every Grafana rule in GrafanaGroupLoader and FilterView. Before this PR, GrafanaRuleLoader passed `rule={rulerRule}` and both actions were available.
